area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the lazy eight point by point (45°, 90°, 135° and 180°), the aerodynamics behind its constantly changing control pressures, and its energy trade, demonstrate symmetrical loops from the right seat while talking them through (about 30° of bank at the steepest point; altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and heading ±10° at each 180° point), and spot and fix your learners' errors.
why: The lazy eight is the one standard training maneuver in which the control pressures never stop changing, so it shows, more clearly than anything else, whether a pilot coordinates by feel across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Mismanaging altitude and airspeed feeds the three most common types of fatal accident, including loss of control and CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. As the instructor you have to fly it smoothly while talking, see which point of the eight went wrong, and turn that into one short, useful correction.

prereading.what: The lazy eight: the pencil picture, the 45°, 90° and 135° reference points, the rudder paragraph, entry power and speed, and the 13 common errors. Read it twice and mark every verb that describes a change.
prereading.label: AFH 10-6 to 10-7

prereading.what: Why performance maneuvers wait for solid fundamentals; lift components, adverse yaw, slip and skid, posture, parallax and rudder timing cues.
prereading.label: AFH 10-1, 3-12 to 3-16

prereading.what: Energy management: the airplane as an energy system, the throttle as total energy controller, the elevator as energy distribution controller, and the three control rules.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-4, 4-10

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls, VA and VO with weight, recovery, and the cross-control stall.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

prereading.what: P-factor, limit load factors, stall speed and load factor, VA, the PHAK note on chandelles and lazy eights, and the rate of turn formula.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-32 to 5-39

prereading.what: How motor skills are learned: stages of skill acquisition, knowledge of results, plateaus, deliberate, blocked and random practice, fixation and inattention.
prereading.label: AIH 3-24 to 3-31

prereading.what: Demonstration, the follow-along exchange of controls, distractions, integrated instruction, see and avoid, correcting errors, and teaching at the right time and altitude.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-12, 10-8

warmup: Think first: you are watching from the right seat. Your learner's first lazy eight to the right looks fine to the 45° point, then the nose drops fast through the horizon, the bank goes past 35° and the ball slides to the right. By the 180° point the airplane is 150 feet low and 15 knots fast. Which of those things went wrong first, which ones are just results of the first, and what one short phrase would you say during the next loop?

key_terms.def: Two opposing 180° turns, each with a climb in its first 90° and a descent in its second 90°, so the airplane's longitudinal axis draws a figure eight lying on its side across the horizon [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
Prominent points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° from the heading at the start of each 180° turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Where the bank is greatest (about 30°), the airspeed lowest (about 5 to 10 knots above stall) and the pitch passes through level [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
The rising wing makes more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn; rudder in the direction of turn cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
At a high angle of attack the downward moving propeller blade takes a bigger bite than the upward moving one, yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Rudder used with aileron so there is no slip or skid; in a skid you feel pushed outward, in a slip inward [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Any stall at more than +1 G, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
The highest speed at which the limit load can be imposed by gusts or full deflection of the controls without structural damage; it goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
The throttle: by setting thrust against drag it decides whether total energy (altitude plus airspeed) rises, falls or stays the same [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
The elevator: it shares the airplane's energy between altitude and airspeed by setting pitch attitude [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
A stretch where progress seems to stop after early fast improvement; normal when learning motor skills [[25:76|AIH 3-25]] [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].
Blocked: the same drill over and over, better short-term scores but poorer long-term learning. Random: skills mixed through the session, better retention [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the CFI standard

body.p: Purpose: the lazy eight develops coordination of the flight controls across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes, and it is the only standard training maneuver in which control pressures are constantly changing [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Like the other performance maneuvers, it also builds planning, situational awareness and division of attention [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

The AFH explains it with a maneuver your learner already knows: S-turns across a road are two opposing 180° turns, and the lazy eight adds a climb to the first 90° and a descent to the second 90° of each one [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

Procedure in one breath: clear the area, pick reference points on the horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° for each 180° turn, set power so the entry speed does not exceed the manufacturer's recommendation (generally not above VA or VO), start a gradual climbing turn, and arrive at the 180° point with wings and nose level at the original airspeed. Then start the climbing turn the other way at once [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: What is new for you: the skills section says you 'demonstrate and simultaneously explain', the knowledge section adds common errors (K5), and S7 means the examiner will fly a flawed lazy eight for you to diagnose. The numbers themselves are the same ones your commercial learner is held to (ACS CA.V.D.S5a to S5e). The private ACS has no lazy eight, so this is a commercial and CFI maneuver.

callout.text: For ASEL, the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, including Task C (Chandelles) or Task D (Lazy Eights) (ACS Area IX note). Prepare both; the chandelle lesson (AI.IX.C) covers the other one, and steep turns (AI.IX.A) cover load factor in depth.

check.q: Your commercial learner asks whether your CFI checkride lazy eight has tighter numbers than theirs. What do you tell them?
check.a: No. Both ACSs ask for approximately 30° at the steepest point and, at each 180° point, altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and heading ±10° (ACS AI.IX.D.S5, CA.V.D.S5). What the CFI test adds is explaining while flying and analyzing and correcting errors (ACS AI.IX.D.S7).

chunks.title: Phases point by point: entry to recovery

body.p: From the pilot's seat, think of the longitudinal axis as a pencil. It draws a symmetrical eight on its side, part above and part below the horizon, and it takes both 180° turns to draw both loops [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. That is why a lazy eight is graded on symmetry and not only on the numbers at the 180° points.

body.p: Approximately 30° bank at the steepest point (S5a) is the only bank number the ACS grades, and the steepest point is the 90° point. The 15° marks at 45° and 135° come from the AFH and are sight-picture aids [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

Phases from entry to recovery: entry from level flight, the climbing turn to the top, the descending turn to the 180° point, the second half the other way, and after the number of symmetrical loops specified, recovery to straight-and-level flight (ACS AI.IX.D.S6). Between the 135° and 180° points the pilot judges the turn remaining and adjusts the rate of rollout and pitch so wings and nose are level at the original airspeed just as the 180° point arrives [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

callout.text: 45: highest. 90: level, steepest, slowest. 135: lowest. 180: level, entry speed, entry altitude.

Have the learner say the points out loud before the flight and on the first loops. You will hear whether the plan is wrong (a knowledge problem) or the plan is right and the airplane does not follow (a skill problem) [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner reaches the 90° point with the nose still well above the horizon and only 20° of bank. What should the picture have been, and what did they skip?
check.a: At 90° the pitch should be passing through level with about 30° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. They skipped letting the nose start down slowly after the 45° point while the bank kept increasing [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Aerodynamics: why the pressures never stop changing

body.p: Constant change of pitch and roll rate and airspeed (S5b) is not decoration; it is the aerodynamics of the maneuver. Pitch, bank and airspeed change all the way around, so the control pressures needed to fly it change all the way around too [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

bullets: Speed and turn rate: as the pitch rises the airspeed falls, and that makes the rate of turn increase. So the roll-in starts slowly, or the 45° point arrives before the highest pitch [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

The formula behind it: rate of turn (degrees per second) = 1,091 x tangent of bank / true airspeed in knots; at a given bank, less speed means a faster turn [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Application: 15° at 100 knots gives about 2.9° per second, but 30° at 55 knots gives about 11.5° per second, roughly four times as fast.
Lift in a bank: total lift splits into a vertical part and a horizontal part, and the horizontal part turns the airplane, not the rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

Overbanking at the top: in some conditions slight opposite aileron is needed at the 90° point to keep the bank from increasing, while rudder still cancels the left-turning tendencies [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Loads: the load factor depends directly on the speed of the dives and the abruptness of the pull-ups; the better the maneuver is flown, the lower the load factor [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

callout.text: Teaching line (application): 'In this maneuver nothing is ever held. If your hands and feet stop moving, the airplane is about to get ahead of you.'

check.q: Your learner says the turn 'runs away' near the top. Explain why in one sentence.
check.a: At the top the airspeed is lowest while the bank is steepest, and at a given bank the rate of turn rises as speed falls [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

chunks.title: Coordination: the rudder through each loop

body.p: How to maintain coordinated flight: the rudder's purpose is to coordinate the turn. Rolling with aileron gives the rising wing more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn; rudder applied with the aileron cancels that adverse yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The AFH says the lazy eight takes substantial skill in coordinating aileron and rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

The second yaw source is P-factor. At a high angle of attack the downward moving blade bites more than the upward moving one and yaws the nose to the left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. In the lazy eight the angle of attack is highest near the slow top, with climb power still set.

head: Part of the loop
Rudder
Why
rows: Climbing toward the top, airspeed falling (both directions)
Gradually more right rudder
Counteracts left-turning tendencies such as P-factor [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Rolling right at low airspeed and high power
Substantial right rudder
Left adverse yaw from the raised left wing adds to left-yawing P-factor [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Rolling left, or in a left climbing turn
Less right rudder
Left-yawing P-factor tends to cancel the adverse yaw to the right [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]

Keep rudder for left-turning tendencies; in some flight conditions, slight opposite aileron to stop overbanking

body.p: Reading the ball: if the ball is not centered, press the rudder on the side the ball has gone to ('step on the ball'). Too little right rudder in a right turn gives a slip, with the ball to the inside of the turn; too much gives a skid, with the ball to the outside [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

Timing cues you can see from the right seat: if the nose starts to move before the bank, rudder is coming in too soon; if the bank starts first or the nose swings the wrong way, rudder is too late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

callout.text: Right, slow, high power: lots of right rudder. Left: less. Speeding up: less.

check.q: From the right seat you see the ball well to the right as your learner rolls right at the slow top. Which pedal, and why is it worst in this direction?
check.a: Right rudder: step on the ball [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Rolling right, left adverse yaw adds to left-yawing P-factor, so the right rudder need is greatest there [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Uncoordinated flight: from a ball out of center to a spin

body.p: Uncoordinated flight in a skid presses the pilot toward the outside of the turn, and in a slip toward the inside; with time a pilot should sense either one without leaning on the instruments [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Warn your learner that body feel can mislead: a skid, a slip and an uncoordinated turn can all feel like the same sideways push [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

bullets: Holding uncoordinated control deflections creates the potential for a spin, and that is most hazardous at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

A cross-control stall happens when the critical angle of attack is exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with very little warning, roll toward inverted and start a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
If the airplane is uncoordinated when it stalls, the bank may change until the angle of attack is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Where it bites in a lazy eight (application of the AFH rudder table): the top is slow, at a high angle of attack, with the most rudder of the loop being used and changed. A learner who carries the heavy right rudder of the right loop into the left loop, or who never adds it in the right loop, is uncoordinated exactly where the stall margin is smallest.

callout.text: Coach the feet before the stall warning, not after. The ball at the top of each loop is the single best check of whether your rudder teaching is working (application).

check.q: Why is a ball out of center more dangerous at the top of a lazy eight than at the 180° point?
check.a: At the top the airspeed is only 5 to 10 knots above stall [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and exceeding the critical angle of attack while uncoordinated can cause a bank change, a roll toward inverted and a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Establish the recommended entry configuration, power, and airspeed (S3). The AFH says to set power so the entry airspeed does not exceed the manufacturer's recommendation, generally no greater than VA or VO [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; Figure 10-4 says maneuvering or cruise speed, whichever is less, or the manufacturer's speed [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. The PHAK puts the recommended entry speed generally near design maneuvering speed, which allows the most load factor without exceeding the load limits [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Configuration (flaps, mixture and so on) comes from the POH.

bullets: VA changes with weight: the FAA example is 100 knots heavily loaded but 90 knots lightly loaded [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Know how VA or VO changes with weight [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Flying at or below VA protects against one full control input in one axis in smooth air, not against several full inputs or inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Older general aviation airplanes: VA is about 1.7 times the normal stall speed; newer designs list it in the AFM/POH [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Limit load factors: normal category 3.8 to -1.52, utility 4.4 to -1.76, acrobatic 6.0 to -3.00 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
A lazy eight pull-up above 2 G does not gain as much altitude, and in a low-powered airplane it may give a net loss; the smoothest pull-up gives the best performance [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
The lowest speed of the maneuver is at the top, about 5 to 10 knots above stall [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
High speed dives or acrobatics above maneuvering speed should never be practiced in rough or turbulent air [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

callout.text: Teaching move (application): in the ground brief, have the learner find the POH entry speed and VA for today's weight and say both out loud. It turns S3 into planning instead of a number on a card.

check.q: Your learner wants to enter at cruise speed 'to get a bigger climb.' What two limits do you point to?
check.a: The entry speed should not exceed the manufacturer's recommendation, generally VA or VO, which drops with weight [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]; and a hard pull-up above 2 G gives less altitude, not more [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Energy management: the throttle sets the total, the elevator trades

body.p: Energy management: the airplane's mechanical energy is the sum of potential energy (altitude) and kinetic energy (airspeed) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. The throttle is the total energy controller and the elevator is the energy distribution controller; neither one controls altitude or airspeed by itself [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

A lazy eight is mostly an energy exchange. Pitching up trades speed for altitude and pitching down trades it back [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Total energy at the end of an exchange can stay the same, as long as thrust is adjusted to match drag as drag changes with airspeed [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. That is why the AFH says power and bank have a big effect: excess power for the bank used gains altitude by the end of the maneuver, and too little loses it [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Energy height: total energy divided by weight, ES = h + V²/2g, measured in feet. It is the height the airplane would reach by trading all its speed for altitude [[24:93|AFH 4-7]] [[24:94|AFH 4-8]]. Application: with V in feet per second (1 knot = 1.688 feet per second) and g = 32.17, slowing from 100 to 92 knots frees (168.8² - 155.3²) / (2 x 32.17) = about 68 feet of altitude.

Use the 180° point as an energy checkpoint (application of AFH chapter 4): altitude and airspeed both high means too much total energy, so too much power for the bank; both low means too little power.
Altitude high but airspeed low (or the reverse) means total energy is about right but it is in the wrong tank: a pitch and rollout problem, not a power problem (application).
Change the power between eights, not in the middle of one (application; the AFH gives no rule for when).
The altimeter and airspeed indicator are the energy instruments: indicated altitude above sea level and indicated airspeed, not height above the ground or groundspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Mismanaging altitude and airspeed contributes to loss of control in flight, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

callout.text: Throttle fills or drains the tank. Elevator pours it between altitude and airspeed.

check.q: Why does the AFH call the elevator an energy distribution controller instead of an altitude control?
check.a: Because pitch only shares the existing energy between vertical flight path and airspeed; changes in total energy come from the throttle setting thrust against drag [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

chunks.title: Accelerated stalls at the slow top

body.p: Accelerated stalls: a stall at any load above +1 G is an accelerated maneuver stall and comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and the most load factor the wing can make before it stalls varies with the square of the airspeed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

Put that at the top of a lazy eight: airspeed is at its minimum, about 5 to 10 knots above stall, and the bank is about 30° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Application: a level 30° turn already needs about 1.15 G, so there is very little left. A learner who pulls to stop the nose falling through the horizon (one of the listed errors) can use up that margin in a second [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Recovery: forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive, come at unexpected airspeeds or pitch attitudes, and can surprise an inexperienced pilot; failure to recover at once may lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Stalling at any point during the maneuver is on the AFH error list [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
An increased load factor raises the stall speed and makes stalls possible at seemingly safe speeds [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

callout.text: Decide before the flight (application): any stall warning in a lazy eight means recover first and teach later. Brief it so the learner expects you to say it.

check.q: Why can a lazy eight stall at an airspeed your learner thinks is safe?
check.a: Any added back pressure raises the load factor, and stall speed rises with its square root [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]; at the top the margin is only 5 to 10 knots to begin with [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Clearing the area and collision hazards

body.p: Clear the area: clearing procedures should come before all turns, including chandelles and lazy eights [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]]. The clearing turn makes sure the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's path, and the instructor should teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. During instruction, have the learner say 'clear left, right, above, and below' out loud [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

bullets: Collision hazards: scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, each area watched at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Wings and door posts hide parts of the sky; move your head, and at times maneuver, such as lifting a wing, to see around them [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Smoke, haze, dust and flying toward the sun greatly reduce the ability to see other aircraft [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]; practice areas can be crowded too [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
A target with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver is a listed lazy eight error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: Teach the habit, not just the clearing turn. Learners who think the instructor handles all the scanning never build constant vigilance, and any tendency to start a maneuver without checking for traffic should be corrected at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Tell the learner you are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Application: a lazy eight climbs, descends and turns both ways, and the learner's eyes are drawn to three reference points; remind them that the reference points are where the eyes go between scans, not instead of them.

check.q: Your learner keeps staring at the 90° reference point through the whole climbing turn. Which listed error is that likely to become?
check.a: Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; have them scan in short 10° steps between glances at the references [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: Select an altitude that keeps the whole maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.D.S2). The altimeter shows height above mean sea level, not above the ground, and height above the ground changes with the terrain [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. So the learner has to know the terrain and obstacle height under the practice area and add the margin, and an error of 100 feet at a 180° point should not take the airplane under the floor (application).

bullets: Low altitude maneuvering, including stall and spin: held uncoordinated deflections create the potential for a spin, especially at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]], and a cross-control stall can be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A sudden loss of control from a steep turn or an abrupt pull near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT): mismanaging altitude and airspeed contributes to CFIT and to loss of control in flight [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Do not teach at an inappropriate altitude, one that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Before a maneuver, prompt the learner to name the collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Application: pick a practice area over flat terrain with a known elevation and a landing field in sight. A learner absorbed in reference points over rising ground is the CFIT setup this element is about.

check.q: Your learner says, 'The altimeter reads 2,600, we're fine for lazy eights.' What is missing?
check.a: The terrain elevation. The altimeter reads MSL, not AGL [[24:87|AFH 4-1]], and the ACS floor is 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.D.S2).

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and disorientation

body.p: Division of attention between aircraft control and orientation: performance maneuvers are built to develop it [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. In any turn the pilot references the natural horizon, scans for traffic and occasionally cross-checks the instruments [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Teach the lazy eight with both outside and instrument references from the first lesson [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], but flying it mainly by the instruments instead of the visual references is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Fixation: absorption in one task while the others slip, often because the task has had too little practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Spot it by glancing at the learner's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Task prioritization: before learners juggle tasks, each task should be done reasonably well on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Budgeting time and prioritizing tasks gives room to work without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness: situational awareness includes the airplane's position and flight path [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]; in a lazy eight that means knowing which reference point comes next. Poor selection or use of the 45°, 90° and 135° references is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: Distractions: in the cognitive stage a skill takes all the learner's attention, and distractions make performance fall apart or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Deliberate practice works best without distractions [[25:77|AIH 3-26]], but that is different from the legitimate use of distractions to teach attention management once the skills are partly mastered [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted, so the most effective training creates distractions during practice maneuvers [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

bullets: Disorientation: sloping cloud formations or an obscured horizon can create a false horizon [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]; do not let the learner pick a cloud edge as a reference point.
The body cannot tell gravity from the accelerations of maneuvering [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]; in the lazy eight's constant changes, trust the horizon and the ball, not the seat.
The leans: an abrupt correction of a bank entered too slowly to be sensed can feel like banking the other way [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

check.q: When in your training plan would you add a distraction to lazy eight practice, and why not on day one?
check.a: Once the learner flies them reasonably well. Early on the skill needs all their attention and distractions make it fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]; later, distractions teach attention management [[25:78|AIH 3-27]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

body.p: Start on the ground and on solid fundamentals. Performance maneuvers wait until the pilot is consistent in the basics, every one starts with a detailed ground lesson, and the training uses segmented building blocks with enough repetition [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. Use the known-to-unknown strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: the AFH itself builds the lazy eight out of S-turns across a road [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

head: Lesson step
Lazy eight application
rows: Ground brief
Objective and standard, the point-by-point picture, the rudder story, the energy trade, safety, and the exchange of controls [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
You fly and explain
Explain power settings, attitudes and other factors as you fly, in the order you briefed [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner follows along
Demonstrate again with the learner following along on the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; in a maneuver whose pressures never stop changing, feeling them is the lesson [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]
Learner flies, you follow along
The learner performs while you follow along on the controls, ready to take over on the first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Debrief
Learner self-assessment first, then yours; concrete suggestions [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

bullets: Brief long, coach short: a long, detailed explanation is confusing before the learner has tried the skill, while specific comments mean more once it is partly mastered [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. During deliberate practice, feedback should be brief and explicit [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

Knowledge of results: tell learners when they are right as well as wrong, soon after the performance, and do not let them practice mistakes; repeating the demonstration and showing the standard helps [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

Plateaus: after fast early progress a plateau is normal for motor skills. Warn the learner, move to another part of the syllabus for a while, and know that over-practice can cause one [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].
Blocked practice (the same drill over and over) scores well today but fools both learner and instructor; random practice, mixing skills, retains better [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].
A beginning learner reaches a point where more practice is unproductive or harmful; errors increase and motivation drops [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

callout.text: Application: plan a few sets of lazy eights, then a different maneuver, then come back, instead of one long string of eights.

check.q: After ten lazy eights in a row your learner is getting worse. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: A beginning learner reaches a point where more practice is unproductive or harmful [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]; switch to something else and come back, and if it is a plateau, explain that it is normal [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

chunks.title: Demonstrating and talking it through from the right seat

body.p: On the CFI test you demonstrate and simultaneously explain (ACS AI.IX.D skills). A lazy eight gives you about a minute of constant change to talk through, so script it and practice the script until talking costs you nothing. Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, clearing included, because learners imitate you [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Where
What you might say (application)
Based on
rows: Before entry
'Clear left, right, above and below. References at 45, 90 and 135. Entry speed set.'
'Slow roll, nose rising; highest pitch right at 45 with about 15 of bank.'
'Nose easing down, bank still increasing, more right rudder as we slow.'
'Level pitch, about 30 of bank, slowest point. No pause.'
'Rolling out slowly, nose to its lowest at 135, less right rudder as speed builds.'
'Watch the turn left; wings and nose level at entry speed just as we reach 180.'
'Altitude, airspeed, heading check. Now the other way.'

body.p: Your view is not your learner's. The AFH describes parallax for a pilot sitting left of the roll axis: the nose seems to rise in a left turn and drop in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: from the right seat the effect is reversed, so your pitch picture differs from the learner's. Sit upright; leaning away from the turn spoils the visual references [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

bullets: Brief the exchange of controls before flight; during the learner's first attempts, guard the controls and be ready to take over [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
If you need the airplane, take it and calmly say 'I have the flight controls'; nothing is gained by fighting an anxious learner on the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
If your demonstration does not match your explanation, say so and explain why at once [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

check.q: Why have the learner follow along lightly on the controls during your second demonstration?
check.a: The AIH sequence is: demonstrate, then have the learner follow along during a demonstration, then the learner flies with you following along [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. In a maneuver where pressures constantly change [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], feeling them is the point.

body.p: The AFH lists 13 common lazy eight errors [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. For S7 the examiner will fly some of them as your learner: name the error, say what caused it, and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not clearing the area
Rolls into the first climbing turn with no clearing turns or calls
Insist on a clearing procedure before every maneuver; correct it at once [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Maneuver is not symmetrical across each 180°
One loop climbs higher or reaches its top sooner than the other
Same reference spacing and the same highest and lowest pitch both ways; mind the rudder difference left and right [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Inadequate or improper selection or use of 45°, 90°, 135° references
Vague points, points on clouds, or the learner loses track of the next one
Pick prominent points on the natural horizon before entry [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; avoid sloping clouds [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Ineffective planning
45° point arrives before the highest pitch; wings level well before 180°
Slow initial roll rate; judge the turn remaining and adjust rollout and pitch rate [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Gain or loss of altitude at each 180° point
Off entry altitude by more than 100 feet
Adjust power for the bank used: excess power gains altitude, too little loses it [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Poor control at the top of each climb segment resulting in the pitch rapidly falling through the horizon
Nose drops fast just after the 90° point
From 45° let the pitch decrease slowly so it passes level at 90°, then keep the rollout slow [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Airspeed or bank angle standards not met
Bank well past 30° at the top; airspeed more than 10 knots off at 180°
Slight opposite aileron if it overbanks at the top; arrive level at the original airspeed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Control roughness
Jerky, large inputs; the airplane lurches between points
Smaller inputs give slower roll rates and time to correct [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]; smooth pull-ups perform better [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]
Poor flight control coordination
Ball out of center, especially at the slow top
Right rudder increasing as speed falls and decreasing as it builds; watch nose versus bank timing [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Stalling at any point during the maneuver
Stall warning or buffet near the top
Recover first: reduce angle of attack, level wings, coordinate, power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; then coach a slower roll and less pull
Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Bank builds quickly while the nose barely rises
More pitch, slow roll: only about 15° of bank at the 45° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver
Eyes locked on a reference point
Scan in short steps between reference glances [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references
Eyes inside on the attitude indicator and airspeed
Horizon first with a quick cross-check [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]; watch the learner's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]

body.p: Where the ACS checks it: at each 180° point, altitude ±100 feet from entry altitude (S5c), airspeed ±10 knots from entry airspeed (S5d) and heading ±10° (S5e), through the number of symmetrical loops specified (S6). Look at the shape too: a loop that is high and slow at one top and flat at the other fails symmetry even when the 180° numbers pass.

How to analyze: when the learner narrates while flying, you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but do not let the same error be practiced over and over [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. To reteach, demonstrate again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Fix the first error in the chain. A fast roll-in (planning) makes the 45° point come early, which makes a rushed top, which makes the nose fall and the airspeed and altitude miss at 180°. Coaching the 180° numbers alone fixes nothing (application).

check.q: Your learner's right loops top out high and slow while the left loops are flat. Which AFH error, and what do you coach?
check.a: The maneuver is not symmetrical across each 180° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Coach the same highest and lowest pitch at the same reference points both ways, and check the rudder, which differs left and right [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

f1.caption: Figure 10-4. Lazy eight. (AFH 10-6)
f1.alt: A light airplane flies a blue ribbon path across a road in the countryside. Starting at A in level flight, it climbs in a turn past B at the 45° point, reaches the top at C at the 90° point with about 30° of bank, descends past D at the 135° point, and is level again at E at the 180° point before turning the other way. Yellow boxes list pitch, bank, speed and altitude at each point.

f2.caption: Figure 3-12. The rudder opposes adverse yaw to help coordinate the turn. (AFH 3-13)
f2.alt: A light airplane rolling into a left turn over a town. The rising right wing has a large More lift arrow and additional induced drag; the lowered left wing has a Reduced lift arrow. A red arrow at the nose shows adverse yaw, and a box says the rudder opposes adverse yaw to coordinate the turn.

f3.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f3.alt: Two side views of an airplane nose. At low angle of attack the load arrows on the upward and downward moving propeller blades are equal. At high angle of attack the airplane is nose high and the arrow on the downward moving blade is larger than the one on the upward moving blade.

f4.caption: Figure 4-3. The reservoir analogy illustrating the primary role of the throttle and elevator to manage the airplane's energy state. (AFH 4-4)
f4.alt: A pipe diagram. Energy gain enters on the left through a valve labeled throttle as thrust, and energy loss leaves on the right as drag. A vertical pipe labeled net energy flow, thrust minus drag, leads down to a valve labeled elevator that connects two tanks: Altitude (potential energy) on the left and Airspeed (kinetic energy) on the right, with arrows showing flow both ways between them.

f5.caption: Figure 5-54. Load factor changes stall speed. (PHAK 5-35)
f5.alt: Two linked graphs. Left: the ratio of accelerated to unaccelerated stall speed rises along a curve as G load goes from 0 to 8. Right: straight lines for unaccelerated stall speeds of 40 to 150 knots convert that ratio to an accelerated stall speed. A dashed green example goes up from 3 G to a ratio of about 1.7, across to a point between the 40 and 50 knot lines, and down to about 75 knots.

f6.caption: Figure 3-17. Learners will probably experience a learning plateau at some point in their training. (AIH 3-25)
f6.alt: A graph of percentage of correct performances against periods of practice. The curve rises quickly from about 46 to 58 percent by period 3, stays nearly flat near 59 to 60 percent from period 3 to 5 at an arrow labeled Plateau, then climbs again to 70 percent at period 8.

f7.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f7.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator in a turn, a turn coordinator, and a seated pilot. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the outside. Coordinated: ball centered and the pilot pressed straight down. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the inside.

scenario.title: First lazy eight lesson with a commercial learner
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your commercial learner flew chandelles well last week and is keen. Today you plan the first lazy eights in a four-seat trainer with just the two of you and half fuel, so the airplane is well under maximum weight. The practice area is hazy, its terrain is about 1,000 feet MSL, a ridge rises to the north, and another school airplane is working nearby. Your learner learns fast but tends to grip the yoke hard when the airspeed gets low.

questions.q: How do you choose the entry altitude, and what does the learner need to know first?
questions.a: Terrain and obstacle elevation from the chart, because the altimeter reads MSL, not AGL [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Then an entry altitude high enough that even a 100-foot low 180° point stays at or above 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.D.S2). Away from the ridge, with a landing field identified [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: The airplane is far below maximum weight today. Which speed goes on your briefing card, and why not the book VA?
questions.a: The POH speed, and not above VA or VO for today's weight [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

questions.q: The learner wants the whole rudder theory explained during the first loop. What do you do instead?
questions.a: Cover P-factor, adverse yaw and the rudder table on the ground; long explanations confuse before the learner has tried the skill, and short comments work better in flight [[25:75|AIH 3-24]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

questions.q: Near the top of the first right loop the ball is far right, the airspeed is 6 knots above stall, and the learner pulls to stop the nose dropping. What is happening and what do you say?
questions.a: Too little right rudder for the slow right roll, where adverse yaw and P-factor add [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], plus a pull that raises the stall speed [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Say 'relax the pull, right rudder, keep it moving'; if the stall warning sounds, recover first [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: The other trainer appears as a speck that stays in the same place on the windshield and slowly grows. What now?
questions.a: No relative motion and growing in size means a likely collision course; take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Then resume scanning, since there may be other aircraft, and make clear you are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: On the way home the learner asks why the ACS bothers with a maneuver no one uses on a trip. What do you say?
questions.a: It builds coordination across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes, with control pressures that never stop changing [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and energy management, whose failure contributes to loss of control and CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

skills.do: Clear the area and explain the clearing as you do it, including where the reference points are.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns and call 'clear left, right, above, and below' on every practice flight, then make your mock learner do the calls [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL), and explain how you got it from the terrain elevation.
skills.practice: Before each flight, find the terrain and obstacle elevation in the practice area and work out the entry altitude out loud [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

skills.do: Establish the recommended entry configuration, power, and airspeed, and explain why that speed for today's weight.
skills.practice: Look up the POH entry speed and VA for the actual weight before every lazy eight flight [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

skills.do: Maintain coordinated flight throughout the maneuver while explaining the changing rudder: more right rudder as speed falls, most when rolling right, less as speed builds.
skills.practice: Fly eights calling the ball position at each reference point; have a partner watch the ball at the top [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Fly about 30° of bank at the steepest point with constant change of pitch, roll rate and airspeed, and at each 180° point hold altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and heading ±10°, while talking.
skills.practice: Practice the point-by-point script from the right seat until you can say it without losing altitude [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Continue the maneuver through the number of symmetrical loops specified, then resume straight-and-level flight.
skills.practice: Have a partner tell you the number of loops in flight, and judge symmetry by comparing the highest and lowest pitch picture left and right [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: watch an examiner-flown flawed lazy eight, name the error, find the first error in the chain, give the fix, and take control if safety requires.
skills.practice: Have another CFI applicant fly each AFH error on purpose while you diagnose it aloud [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Which ground reference maneuver does the AFH use to explain the lazy eight?
options: Turns around a point on the ground
Rectangular course
Eights on pylons
S-turns across a road
quiz.why: The AFH compares it to S-turns across the road, two opposing 180° turns, with a climb and a descent added to each [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

quiz.q: Where in each 180° turn should the lowest pitch attitude occur?
options: At the 135° point
At the 90° point
At the 180° point
Just after the 45° point
quiz.why: When the airplane has turned 135° it should be at its lowest pitch attitude [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: As the pitch rises in the first 45°, the airspeed falls. What does that do to the rate of turn at a given bank?
options: It increases, so the 45° point can come early
It stays the same; only bank changes it
It decreases, so the 45° point comes later than planned
It decreases because drag rises with pitch
quiz.why: Decreasing airspeed makes the rate of turn increase, so a fast roll-in can reach the 45° point before the highest pitch [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

quiz.q: Why does rolling left near the top take less right rudder than rolling right?
options: Left aileron makes almost no adverse yaw at low airspeed
Left-yawing P-factor tends to cancel the adverse yaw
Engine torque is weaker during left climbing turns
The left wing stalls first, so the rudder is blanked
quiz.why: Rolling left, the adverse yaw is to the right and left-yawing P-factor tends to cancel it, so less right rudder is needed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: The POH lists VA at maximum weight. Today you are well below it. What happens to VA?
options: It goes down as weight goes down
It is fixed for the airplane
It changes only with altitude
It goes up as weight goes down
quiz.why: VA decreases with weight; the FAA example is 100 knots heavy and 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

quiz.q: At each 180° point your learner is right on altitude but 12 knots slow. In energy terms, what happened?
options: Total energy rose: too much power was used for the bank
Total energy rose because the bank was too shallow
Nothing: the elevator only moved energy between tanks
Total energy fell: too little power for the bank used
quiz.why: Same altitude with less airspeed means less total energy; the throttle controls total energy, and too little power for the bank used loses energy [[24:90|AFH 4-4]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a stall at the top of a lazy eight is true?
options: Any added back pressure raises the stall speed above 1 G
Climbing lowers the stall speed below its 1 G value
A stall cannot happen with less than 45° of bank
The airplane always breaks straight ahead, coordinated or not
quiz.why: Stalls above +1 G come at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; an uncoordinated stall may change the bank [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: The AIM gives one way to see sky hidden by a wing or door post. What is it?
options: Rely on the traffic display alone
Climb 500 feet before each loop
Turn on every light the airplane has
Move your head and at times lift a wing
quiz.why: Pilots need to move their heads to see around blind spots and at times maneuver, such as lifting a wing [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

quiz.q: Your learner is still at the stage where a lazy eight takes all their attention. What will a distraction do now?
options: Improve retention through random practice
Speed up the move to automatic flying
Usually make the performance fall apart
Nothing, if the distraction is short
quiz.why: In the cognitive stage, distractions introduced by an instructor often cause performance to deteriorate or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Which AFH error matches a nose that drops fast through the horizon just after the top?
options: Poor control at the top of each climb segment
Control roughness
Ineffective planning
Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
quiz.why: The AFH lists poor control at the top of each climb segment resulting in the pitch rapidly falling through the horizon [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: During S7 the examiner, as your learner, reaches the first 180° point 90 feet low, 11 knots fast and 8° off heading. Which item fails?
options: The heading
The altitude
The airspeed
None; all are within standard
final_quiz.why: The standard at the 180° point is ±100 feet, ±10 knots and ±10° (ACS AI.IX.D.S5c to S5e); 11 knots is outside. Airspeed standards not met is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's lazy eights look like 30° steep turns with a small climb. Which coaching fits the AFH?
options: Hold the nose level and let the bank do the turning work
Add power so the climb grows larger while the bank stays the same
Steepen the bank to 45° so the turn finishes much sooner
Raise the pitch more and roll slower, about 15° of bank at 45°
final_quiz.why: Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver is a listed error; the highest pitch comes at 45° with only about 15° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: In a right lazy eight the examiner keeps the rudder neutral while rolling right as the airspeed bleeds off near the top. What do you expect to see?
options: Ball to the left as the nose yaws toward the turn
Ball to the right as adverse yaw and P-factor add
Ball centered, since rudder does little when slow
Ball to the left as P-factor yaws the nose right
final_quiz.why: Rolling right at low airspeed and high power, left adverse yaw adds to left-yawing P-factor and needs substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Too little right rudder in a right turn is a slip, with the ball to the inside of the turn [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

final_quiz.q: From a 100-knot entry your learner reaches the 180° point 70 feet high and 8 knots slow. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Too much power: total energy is far above entry
Total energy about right but left in altitude: fix pitch
Too little power: total energy is far below entry
Uncoordinated flight bled off the extra airspeed
final_quiz.why: Energy height is h + V²/2g [[24:93|AFH 4-7]]. Slowing from 100 to 92 knots frees (168.8² - 155.3²) / (2 x 32.17) = about 68 feet (speeds in feet per second), close to the 70 feet gained, so total energy is about the same and the elevator, the energy distribution controller, left it in altitude [[24:90|AFH 4-4]] [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane stalls at 47 knots at 1 G. At the top, at 52 knots, the learner pulls to 1.5 G to stop the nose falling. What happens?
options: Nothing happens, since 52 knots is still above the 47-knot stall speed
It stalls only if the bank angle is more than 45°
The load factor drops because the airspeed is low
It stalls: at 52 knots the wing can make only about 1.2 G
final_quiz.why: The most load factor before the stall varies with the square of airspeed: (52 / 47)² = 1.22 G [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Asking for 1.5 G stalls the wing, an accelerated stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: After three lessons of quick progress your learner's lazy eights stop improving for two flights, and they are discouraged. What does the AIH advise?
options: Explain that plateaus are normal, and give lazy eights a short break
Add twenty more lazy eights to each flight until the curve starts to rise
Book the checkride, since a plateau means the skill is learned
Drop lazy eights for good and return to S-turns across a road
final_quiz.why: A plateau is normal for motor skills; prepare the learner and move to another part of the curriculum for a while [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

final_quiz.q: You want lazy eights to stick for a checkride in three weeks. Which practice plan does the AIH favor?
options: Twelve lazy eights in a row, every lesson
Lazy eights only on the flight before the test
Lazy eights mixed with other maneuvers
Lazy eights only in a simulator until the test
final_quiz.why: Blocked practice scores well during practice, but random practice that mixes skills does better on a test the next day [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner narrates '45, highest pitch; 90, level and steepest; 135, lowest' correctly, but the airplane reaches each point late. What does that tell you?
options: A misconception: the learner does not really know the points yet
Probably motor skill: the plan is right, the hands lag
Nothing; narration and flying cannot be compared
The ACS tolerance is too tight for this learner
final_quiz.why: When the learner thinks aloud while flying, it is easy to tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: Terrain in the practice area is 1,300 feet MSL. Your learner plans an entry at 2,700 feet MSL. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the climb on each loop adds altitude
The entry is too high for the 1,500-foot floor
The entry is only 1,400 feet AGL, below the floor
Nothing, if the 180° points stay within 100 feet
final_quiz.why: 2,700 - 1,300 = 1,400 feet AGL, below the 1,500-foot AGL floor (ACS AI.IX.D.S2). The altimeter reads MSL, not AGL [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner, as your learner, pauses two seconds at the top with 30° of bank and the nose level. How do you grade it?
options: Fine; the pause lets the airspeed settle
An error: the AFH says not to hesitate at 90°
Only an error in a left lazy eight
Fine, as long as the 180° altitude is within 100 feet
final_quiz.why: The pilot should not hesitate at the 90° point but continue into the descending turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; S5b asks for constant change of pitch, roll rate and airspeed (ACS AI.IX.D.S5b).

final_quiz.q: S3 asks for the 'recommended entry configuration.' Where does your learner find it?
options: In the ACS itself, under S3
In the AFH lazy eight section
In the airplane's POH or AFM
In the PHAK load factor chapter
final_quiz.why: The AFH gives only the entry speed ceiling based on the manufacturer's recommendation [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; configuration is airplane specific and comes from the POH/AFM (ACS references).

final_quiz.q: Your learner repeats the same lopsided loop three times while you say nothing, planning to discuss it later. What does the AIH say?
options: Fine; save all comments for the debrief
Take the controls and fly the rest yourself
Fine, if the 180° numbers are within tolerance
Learners should not be left to practice a mistake
final_quiz.why: Learners should be told as soon after the performance as possible and should not be allowed to practice mistakes; it is harder to unlearn than to learn right [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

final_quiz.q: Right loops top out 250 feet above entry, left loops only 100 feet, and every 180° point is on standard. Which ACS item is the issue?
options: S5c, because the top altitude is graded
S5a, since the bank must be 45° on both
S6, the loops must be symmetrical
None; only the 180° points are graded
final_quiz.why: S6 asks for symmetrical loops (ACS AI.IX.D.S6), and the AFH lists a maneuver not symmetrical across each 180° as an error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

takeaways: CFI and commercial standard: about 30° at the steepest point, constant change, and at each 180° point altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, heading ±10°.
45: highest pitch, about 15°. 90: level pitch, about 30°, slowest. 135: lowest pitch. 180: level, entry speed and altitude.
Right rudder grows as speed falls, is greatest rolling right at the slow top, and shrinks as speed builds.
The throttle sets total energy and the elevator shares it; end high or low, adjust power; end high and slow, fix pitch.
The top is 5 to 10 knots above stall: a pull or a ball out of center there invites an accelerated or cross-control stall.
Brief long on the ground, coach short in the air, and fix the first error in the chain.
Mix lazy eights with other maneuvers, expect a plateau, and stop when more practice makes it worse.
cfi_notes: The ACS grades bank only as approximately 30° at the steepest point (ACS AI.IX.D.S5a). The 15° figures at 45° and 135° come from the AFH text and Figure 10-4 [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]; use them as sight pictures, not as a pass or fail line.

Three sources word the entry speed differently: generally no greater than VA or VO [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], maneuvering or cruise speed whichever is less or the manufacturer's speed [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and generally near VA [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. They agree on the ceiling; teach the POH speed for the day's weight.

The AFH rudder paragraph first says right rudder is needed at the apex 'in both the right and left turns' and then that left turns need less [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. It is not a contradiction, just hard to read; teach the AFH's own summary (rolling right at low airspeed and high power needs substantial right rudder) and let the ball confirm it.

The AFH says medium banks (20° to 45°) hold themselves with neutral aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]], yet says the lazy eight's 30° top may need slight opposite aileron in some conditions [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The low airspeed and changing pitch make the top different; let the airplane show what it needs.

The AIH says learners should not be allowed to practice mistakes [[25:76|AIH 3-25]] and also that, safety permitting, it is often better to let them go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Working rule: let one loop show the error, then correct it before the next one.

The AIH says to avoid distractions during deliberate practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]] and also that the most effective training creates distractions while maneuvers are practiced [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. The AIH reconciles them on 3-27: distractions are for attention management once skills are partly mastered [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

Parallax is described only for the left seat [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. No source here describes the right-seat picture; applying the same geometry it is reversed, so coach from what the learner should see, not from what you see.

The AFH puts the top airspeed 'about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed' without saying which stall speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. A 30° bank and any pull raise the stall speed above the 1 G figure [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], so treat the airspeed indicator as giving less margin than it seems.
Many learners stall progress at about the third lazy eight lesson (application). Tell them in advance that plateaus are normal for motor skills [[25:77|AIH 3-26]] so they do not read it as failure.
gaps: The sources give no pitch attitudes for the 45° and 135° points; they depend on the airplane, power and entry speed. Work them out in the airplane you teach in.
Entry configuration and power setting are not given in the AFH beyond the speed ceiling [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; get them from the POH/AFM.
The ACS says 'the number of symmetrical loops specified' but no source says how many an examiner will ask for; practice at least two full eights.
No source here says whether a lazy eight counts as aerobatic flight under 14 CFR 91.303; the 1,500-foot AGL floor in this lesson comes from the ACS.
No source gives a right-seat sight picture or a script for talking through the maneuver; the script in this lesson is application.
No source here tells a CFI how far to let a lazy eight error run before taking control; the AIH only says 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

activities.title: Grade it and work the margins
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A left lazy eight starts on heading 020. The learner reaches the first 180° point on 213. How many degrees outside the ±10° tolerance is that?
items.why: Turning left 180° from 020: 020 - 180 = -160, so 200. 213 - 200 = 13° off; 13 - 10 = 3° outside (ACS AI.IX.D.S5e).

items.q: Entry altitude 4,500 feet. The first 180° point comes at 4,380 feet. How many feet outside the tolerance?
items.why: 4,500 - 4,380 = 120 feet low; 120 - 100 = 20 feet outside (ACS AI.IX.D.S5c). Too little power for the bank loses altitude [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

items.q: What load factor does a level, coordinated 30° bank need? (1 / cos of the bank)
items.why: cos 30° = 0.866; 1 / 0.866 = 1.155 G. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

items.q: Your airplane stalls at 47 knots at 1 G. A learner yanks to 2 G near the top. At what airspeed would the wing stall?
items.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor: 47 x square root of 2 = 47 x 1.414 = 66.5 knots [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], far above the top's 5 to 10 knot margin [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

items.q: An older general aviation airplane stalls at 52 knots. Using the PHAK rough rule for VA, what is the highest entry speed?
items.why: For older general aviation airplanes VA is about 1.7 times the normal stalling speed: 1.7 x 52 = 88.4 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]; entry should not exceed VA [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

activities.title: Teaching lazy eights, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFI with a commercial learner on their first lazy eight lesson. The airplane is light, and the practice area terrain is about 1,000 feet MSL.

steps.s: Your learner sets up to start at 2,400 feet MSL.
options: Fine; 1,400 feet above the ground is close enough
Descend to 2,000 feet to see the references better
Climb so even a 100-foot low 180° point stays 1,500 feet AGL or higher
Fine, since each loop climbs above the entry altitude
steps.why: The ACS floor is 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.D.S2) and the altimeter reads MSL [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]; 2,400 - 1,000 = 1,400 feet AGL.

steps.s: On the first try the 45° point arrives with the nose still rising and the bank already 20°.
options: Coach more back pressure so the nose rises faster
Coach a slower roll-in so the highest pitch comes at 45°
Tell the learner to pick a reference point farther away
Say nothing; only the 180° point is graded
steps.why: Increasing pitch and bank together can make the turn so fast that 45° arrives before the highest pitch; start with a slow rate of roll [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

steps.s: At the top of the right loop the ball is far right, the speed is 6 knots above stall, and the learner starts pulling to stop the nose dropping.
options: Coach: pull harder to hold the altitude
Coach: add left rudder to center the ball
Coach: relax the pull, right rudder, keep it moving
Coach: pause at the top until the speed settles
steps.why: Ball right means step on the right rudder [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]; rolling right slow needs substantial right rudder and the AFH says not to hesitate at 90° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; a pull raises the stall speed [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

steps.s: After ten lazy eights in a row the errors are increasing and the learner is getting frustrated.
options: Lower the standard so the learner can pass
Keep going until one is perfect
Take the controls and fly the rest yourself
Switch to another maneuver and come back later
steps.why: A beginning learner reaches a point where more practice is unproductive or harmful, and over-practice can bring on a plateau [[25:78|AIH 3-27]] [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

steps.s: Two lessons later the learner flies lazy eights close to standard every time.
options: Add a realistic distraction, such as reading the outside air temperature
Add three distractions at once to test the limits
Never add distractions to lazy eights
Stop practicing; the skill is now automatic
steps.why: Once skills are partly mastered, distractions legitimately teach attention management [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]; reading the OAT is on the AIH list [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

activities.title: True or false: teaching lazy eights
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH says to pause briefly at the 90° point so the airspeed can settle.
cards.why: False. The pilot should not hesitate at the 90° point but continue into the descending turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

cards.s: Over-practice can bring on a learning plateau.
cards.why: True. Instructors can bring on a plateau by over-practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

cards.s: Large aileron and rudder inputs help a beginner feel the changing pressures sooner.
cards.why: False. Large inputs give rapid roll rates and little time to correct; smaller inputs are better [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

cards.s: Flying the lazy eight mainly by the attitude indicator is a listed error.
cards.why: True. Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references is on the AFH list [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

cards.s: The PHAK says lazy eight load factors depend directly on the speed of the dives and the abruptness of the pull-ups.
Picking the edge of a sloping cloud bank as the 90° reference point is a good idea on a hazy day.
cards.why: False. Sloping cloud formations can create a false horizon [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]; use prominent points on the natural horizon [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
